nodes.label: markdownlint rule configuration
nodes.rationale: Defaults on, with line-length (MD013), inline HTML (MD033), fenced-code-language (MD040) and several list/emphasis rules disabled to accommodate MkDocs Material admonitions and long ADR prose; MD024 restricted to siblings_only so repeated Status/Context/Decision headings across ADRs are legal.

nodes.label: autoupdate workflow (merge main into open PRs)
nodes.rationale: Runs on pushes to main; needs contents/pull-requests/workflows write because the action merges the base branch into open PRs.
nodes.norm_label: autoupdate workflow (merge main into open prs)

nodes.label: CI job: build (JDK 21, mvn clean install, Codecov)
nodes.rationale: The H2 build is the required gate; GITHUB_TOKEN is least-privilege contents:read, and JS actions are forced onto Node 24 ahead of the Node 20 removal in Sep 2026.
nodes.norm_label: ci job: build (jdk 21, mvn clean install, codecov)

nodes.label: CI job: dialect-its (advisory Testcontainers ITs)
nodes.rationale: Non-blocking (continue-on-error) real PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB runs via -Pdialect-its; Ryuk is disabled because pulling testcontainers/ryuk fails under Docker Hub rate limits and JUnit 5 @Container lifecycle already reaps containers.

nodes.label: CI job: mutation (blocking PIT run)
nodes.rationale: PIT over failover-core under -Pmutation; the 95% threshold is enforced in the POM so the job fails the check below it, making mutation coverage a blocking gate rather than a report.

nodes.label: Release workflow: publish to Maven Central Portal
nodes.rationale: Triggered on release creation; server-id 'central' must match publishingServerId in the makeRelease profile. GPG passphrase is passed as MAVEN_GPG_PASSPHRASE rather than -Dgpg.passphrase so it never appears in the process argument list; CENTRAL_USERNAME/PASSWORD are Central Portal user tokens, not renamed OSSRH credentials.
nodes.norm_label: release workflow: publish to maven central portal

nodes.label: Failover Library (project overview)
nodes.rationale: Spring Boot library that transparently stores referential service responses and replays the last known-good value when the upstream fails; entry point is @Failover on a concrete class method because the CGLIB proxy requires the annotation on the implementation, not an interface.

nodes.label: Failover Handler Chain
nodes.rationale: AdvancedFailoverHandler (observable reporting, RecoveredPayloadHandler, exception policy) wraps ScatterGatherFailoverHandler (per-entity slicing) wraps DefaultFailoverHandler (store/recover + expiry). Layering keeps each concern independently replaceable and assembled at one point, FailoverAutoConfiguration.failoverHandler.

nodes.label: Store Assembly Chain
nodes.rationale: AsyncFailoverStore wraps MultiTenantFailoverStore wraps the base store (InMemory | Caffeine | JDBC | custom). Ordering is deliberate: tenant routing must sit inside the async decorator so each tenant's store receives identical wrapping.

nodes.label: FailoverStore.find defensive-copy contract
nodes.rationale: find() must return a defensive copy because callers mutate the returned payload (setting upToDate, asOf); without cloning the mutation would corrupt the stored entry.

nodes.label: ConditionalOnMissingBean extension points
nodes.rationale: Every core bean is @ConditionalOnMissingBean so a consumer can replace any default by declaring their own bean; named beans are referenced from @Failover attributes (keyGenerator, expiryPolicy, payloadSplitter, domain).

nodes.label: Module responsibility map
nodes.rationale: One module per concern (domain, core, aspect, per-backend stores, async, multitenant, lookup, resilience, scanner, observable, scheduler, autoconfigure, starter, dashboard) so a consumer only pays for what they add; the dashboard is deliberately self-contained and does not depend on failover-spring-boot-autoconfigure.

nodes.label: Testing conventions (unit vs IT, AssertJ, async=false)
nodes.rationale: Unit tests are pure Mockito/JUnit 5; integration tests live only in failover-spring-boot-autoconfigure against real H2 and set failover.store.async=false so writes are synchronous and assertions deterministic. AssertJ assertThat().isInstanceOf() is mandated over Assert.isInstanceOf().
nodes.norm_label: testing conventions (unit vs it, assertj, async=false)

nodes.label: Security Policy and Supported Versions
nodes.rationale: 3.x fully supported, 2.x critical fixes only, <2.0 unsupported. Vulnerabilities go through private GitHub Security Advisories rather than public issues, acknowledged within 5 business days.

nodes.label: Operator note: JDBC payload deserialization allowlist
nodes.rationale: The JDBC store deserializes by the class name in the PAYLOAD_CLASS column; loading is restricted to an allowlist auto-derived from discovered @Failover payload packages so only the consumer's own referential classes materialize. failover.store.jdbc.allowed-payload-classes is an additive override for types the scanner cannot infer (e.g. a scatter slice type in another package).
nodes.norm_label: operator note: jdbc payload deserialization allowlist

nodes.label: Table-prefix identifier validation
nodes.rationale: failover.store.jdbc.table-prefix and per-tenant prefixes are concatenated into SQL identifiers, so they are validated to contain only letters, digits, underscores and dot-separated qualifiers.

nodes.label: Operator note: multi-tenant strict mode
nodes.rationale: In TABLE_PREFIX mode, failover.store.multitenant.strict=true rejects tenants absent from the configured map, preventing an unconfigured tenant from silently sharing the global store table.

nodes.label: ADR 1 — Build a failover lib
nodes.rationale: Platforms depend on many referential systems whose unavailability makes the platform unusable, and the impact compounds with each dependency. Since referential data changes rarely and business often accepts slightly stale data, keep a local store written on every successful call, recover from it on failure, and bound staleness with a business-agreed expiry plus cleanup. Must stay very simple because it will be adopted by many services.

nodes.label: ADR 2 — Dedicated @Failover annotation
nodes.rationale: Reusing @FeignClient was possible, but a dedicated @Failover annotation reads better at the call site and gives a natural home for the unique name and expiry configuration. Trade-off accepted: it only works through Spring AOP.

nodes.label: ADR 3 — Referential metadata: asOf / upToDate
nodes.rationale: Callers need to know how old recovered data is (asOf) and whether it is live or recovered (upToDate). Delivered as a deliberately tiny domain module (one annotation, one interface, one abstract class); both contracts are optional — no contract applied means no metadata populated.

nodes.label: ADR 4 — RecoveredPayloadHandler SPI
nodes.rationale: Gives consumers a hook to decide what a null/absent recovery means (e.g. return an empty collection instead of null) rather than baking one policy into the handler.

nodes.label: ADR 5 — FailoverStore abstraction and built-in stores
nodes.rationale: Ship basic storage options rather than force every consumer to write one: INMEMORY (ConcurrentHashMap, explicitly not for production), CAFFEINE, JDBC (needs JdbcTemplate + ObjectMapper) and CUSTOM. store and delete may run asynchronously because store I/O otherwise taxes the caller's latency.
nodes.norm_label: adr 5 — failoverstore abstraction and built-in stores

nodes.label: ADR 6 — FailoverExecution SPI (BASIC vs RESILIENCE)
nodes.rationale: Two execution strategies behind one SPI: BASIC try/catch for the zero-dependency case and RESILIENCE for Resilience4j circuit-breaker wrapping, selected by failover.type.

nodes.label: ADR 7 — Scheduled expiry cleanup
nodes.rationale: Expired entries must be reclaimed or the store grows without bound; ExpiryCleanupScheduler runs the delete on a cron rather than on the hot path.

nodes.label: ADR 8 — FailoverReporter monitoring
nodes.rationale: Reporting split behind publishers (logger, Micrometer) so observability backends are pluggable; later renamed to the observer/publisher stack by ADR 29.

nodes.label: ADR 9 — KeyGenerator SPI
nodes.rationale: The store key is derived from method arguments by default, with a named-bean override so consumers can key on something other than the raw argument list.

nodes.label: ADR 10 — DefaultFailoverStore defensive copy
nodes.rationale: Callers mutate the recovered ReferentialPayload (upToDate, asOf), so the store clones on the way out; without the copy the in-memory store would hand out its own live entry and be corrupted by the caller.

nodes.label: ADR 11 — Store wrapping via BeanPostProcessor (Deprecated)
nodes.rationale: Originally wrapped raw FailoverStore beans with DefaultFailoverStore → FailoverStoreAsync via static @Bean BeanPostProcessors. Deprecated once multi-tenancy exposed two fatal flaws (see ADR 16): a BPP only sees Spring-managed beans, and @Async only works through a Spring AOP proxy.

nodes.label: ADR 12 — MethodExceptionPolicy (RETHROW / NEVER_THROW / CUSTOM)
nodes.rationale: What to do when recovery cannot produce a value is a business decision, not a library one — so it is an enum-selected pluggable strategy rather than a hardcoded rethrow.

nodes.label: ADR 13 — JDBC native merge/upsert with dialect detection
nodes.rationale: Dialect-specific single-statement upsert avoids the insert-then-update race and round trip, with an ANSI insert/update fallback for unrecognised databases so no dialect is unsupported.
nodes.norm_label: adr 13 — jdbc native merge/upsert with dialect detection

nodes.label: ADR 14 — DatabaseResolver SPI
nodes.rationale: Database-product detection is isolated behind a strategy interface so dialect selection is testable and overridable rather than being inline metadata sniffing.

nodes.label: ADR 15 — FailoverStoreQueryResolver co-locates JDBC query building
nodes.rationale: All SQL construction (table prefix, dialect merge, column resolution) lives in one single-responsibility collaborator so FailoverStoreJdbc holds execution only.
nodes.norm_label: adr 15 — failoverstorequeryresolver co-locates jdbc query building

nodes.label: ADR 16 — Remove BeanPostProcessor store wrapping (supersedes ADR 11)
nodes.rationale: A BPP only intercepts Spring-managed beans, so per-tenant stores built inside a TenantStoreFactory would silently skip async/defensive-copy wrapping; and @Async on a factory-created instance degrades to synchronous with no error. Wrapping is therefore assembled explicitly at one visible point, and @EnableAsync is removed from the autoconfigure module as the correct responsibility boundary.
nodes.norm_label: adr 16 — remove beanpostprocessor store wrapping (supersedes adr 11)

nodes.label: ADR 17 — TenantStoreFactory SPI
nodes.rationale: Separates per-tenant store creation from store assembly so the assembler does not need to know how a tenant's backend is constructed.

nodes.label: ADR 18 — FailoverStoreAutoConfiguration as central assembler
nodes.rationale: One auto-configuration class owns the whole store chain so the wrapping order is explicit, deterministic and reviewable in a single place instead of emerging from bean-post-processing order.

nodes.label: ADR 19 — FailoverStoreAsync holds an explicit TaskExecutor
nodes.rationale: @Async silently degrades to synchronous when the instance is not a Spring proxy; an injected TaskExecutor works regardless of how the store was constructed and makes the concurrency strategy testable.
nodes.norm_label: adr 19 — failoverstoreasync holds an explicit taskexecutor

nodes.label: ADR 20 — MultiTenantFailoverStore as routing decorator
nodes.rationale: Tenant routing must sit outside the per-tenant wrapping so every tenant's store receives the identical DefaultFailoverStore/async chain; placement relative to the async decorator determines whether the tenant context is resolved on the caller thread.

nodes.label: ADR 21 — Multi-tenant auto-configuration and TenantResolver SPI
nodes.rationale: Multi-tenancy is a separate opt-in auto-configuration so the single-tenant path carries none of its conditionals; how the current tenant is discovered is a TenantResolver SPI because it is application-specific.
nodes.norm_label: adr 21 — multi-tenant auto-configuration and tenantresolver spi

nodes.label: ADR 22 — FailoverKeyGenerator UUID key normalisation
nodes.rationale: Argument-derived keys are unbounded in length and overflow the VARCHAR(256) key column; hashing to a fixed-width MD5/UUID makes every key storable regardless of argument size.

nodes.label: ADR 23 — PayloadSplitter scatter/gather storage
nodes.rationale: Batch-fetch methods keyed on the whole argument suffer subset and superset misses ('1,2,3' misses an entry stored as '1,2,3,4'), so the cache is only useful when callers repeat the exact same id set. Splitting the composite payload into per-entity slices keyed through the same FailoverKeyGenerator chain makes partial recovery possible; opt-in via @Failover(payloadSplitter=...) so the default single-key path is unchanged.

nodes.label: ADR 24 — Parallel scatter/gather via CompletableFuture + injected Executor
nodes.rationale: Sequential dispatch costs the sum of slice latencies (10 slices × 50ms = 500ms). Explicitly rejected ForkJoinPool/parallelStream: slices are I/O-bound and the common pool risks starvation. A SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor with virtual threads avoids platform-pool exhaustion; a null executor keeps the sequential default.
nodes.norm_label: adr 24 — parallel scatter/gather via completablefuture + injected executor

nodes.label: ADR 25 — ContextPropagator SPI for parallel scatter
nodes.rationale: Dispatching slices onto executor threads loses thread-local context (tenant, tracing, MDC); the SPI captures on the caller thread and restores on the worker, with a composite for combining propagators.
nodes.norm_label: adr 25 — contextpropagator spi for parallel scatter

nodes.label: ADR 26 — Instant instead of LocalDateTime for expiry
nodes.rationale: LocalDateTime carries no zone, so expiry computed on one node and evaluated on another in a different timezone is ambiguous; Instant removes the ambiguity for multi-node/multi-timezone deployments.
nodes.norm_label: adr 26 — instant instead of localdatetime for expiry

nodes.label: ADR 27 — Migrate deprecated JdbcTemplate overloads
nodes.rationale: Varargs overloads replace the deprecated Object[] + int[] forms, which also removes the java.sql.Types coupling.

nodes.label: ADR 28 — domain attribute for shared store partitioning
nodes.rationale: A scatter/gather batch endpoint and a single-entity endpoint fetch the same entities but would otherwise write to different partitions; a shared domain lets them share store entries. Mismatched expiry inside one domain is warned at startup.
nodes.norm_label: adr 28 — domain attribute for shared store partitioning

nodes.label: ADR 29 — Observer/Publisher SPI and MDC logger refactor
nodes.rationale: Renames the reporter stack to observer, publishes through an ObservablePublisher SPI with a composite, and makes logging MDC-safe so observability never leaks context across threads.
nodes.norm_label: adr 29 — observer/publisher spi and mdc logger refactor

nodes.label: ADR 30 — SpringContextFailoverScanner replaces Reflections scanning
nodes.rationale: Enumerating Spring beans finds exactly the @Failover methods that are actually advisable, removing the package-to-scan configuration burden and the Reflections/Guava dependency.

nodes.label: ADR 31 — failover-observable-micrometer as an optional module
nodes.rationale: Micrometer meters and the Actuator health indicator are extracted into an opt-in module so core carries no Micrometer dependency.
nodes.norm_label: adr 31 — failover-observable-micrometer as an optional module

nodes.label: ADR 32 — PayloadSplitterExecutionException wrapping
nodes.rationale: A failure inside consumer-written splitter code is otherwise an opaque stack trace; wrapping every call with splitter name and operation context makes the diagnosis obvious.

nodes.label: ADR 33 — doRecoverAll iterates all slices
nodes.rationale: Slice count is user-controlled through splitOnRecover rather than inferred by the framework, so doRecoverAll simply iterates whatever the splitter returns.

nodes.label: ADR 34 — ScatterGatherFailoverHandler.recoverAll() throws
nodes.rationale: Inheriting the default recoverAll in scatter mode would silently execute the wrong path; an explicit UnsupportedOperationException fails loudly instead.

nodes.label: ADR 35 — Empty splitOnRecover returns null, not merge([])
nodes.rationale: Merging an empty list would fabricate an empty successful result indistinguishable from a real one; returning null keeps 'nothing recovered' honest.
nodes.norm_label: adr 35 — empty splitonrecover returns null, not merge([])

nodes.label: ADR 36 — splitOnRecover single-placeholder contract
nodes.rationale: When delegating to DefaultFailoverHandler.recoverAll the splitter must return exactly one placeholder context, making the delegation contract explicit rather than implied.

nodes.label: ADR 37 — Payload deserialization allowlist
nodes.rationale: JsonSerializer.toClass loading an arbitrary class name from a store row is a deserialization-gadget surface; restricting it to an allowlist auto-derived from discovered @Failover payload packages is secure by default with no consumer configuration.

nodes.label: ADR 38 — Scatter/gather per-slice timeout
nodes.rationale: A hung slice would block the caller through allOf().join(); failover.scatter.timeout bounds the join — a timed-out recover slice counts as not recovered, a timed-out store slice surfaces.

nodes.label: ADR 39 — Error propagates unwrapped; never recover on a failing JVM
nodes.rationale: Treating an OutOfMemoryError as an upstream failure would run recovery logic on a dying JVM; the aspect rethrows Error unwrapped instead.
nodes.norm_label: adr 39 — error propagates unwrapped; never recover on a failing jvm

nodes.label: ADR 40 — Multi-tenant strict mode
nodes.rationale: Without strict mode an unconfigured tenant silently falls through to the global table, cross-contaminating data; the flag rejects (or WARNs once on) tenants absent from the map.

nodes.label: ADR 41 — failover.store.async.failed metric
nodes.rationale: The async store is a silently-degrading layer — an executor-side write failure never reaches the caller — so it must publish its own failure counter to be visible at all.

nodes.label: ADR 42 — FailoverScanner moved to a neutral core package
nodes.rationale: The scanner stopped being an observability-only concern once store deserialization safety consumed it, so core.observable.scanner → core.scanner reflects the shared ownership.
nodes.norm_label: adr 42 — failoverscanner moved to a neutral core package

nodes.label: ADR 43 — Dialect integration tests via Testcontainers
nodes.rationale: Dialect-specific merge SQL cannot be validated against H2; real PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB containers exercise it, profile-gated (dialect-its) and excluded from the default build because they need Docker. Oracle stays string-asserted for lack of a freely-pullable image.
nodes.norm_label: adr 43 — dialect integration tests via testcontainers

nodes.label: ADR 44 — Concurrency tests for tenant routing and the async store
nodes.rationale: computeIfAbsent must yield exactly one store per tenant under contention, and the async executor path must not lose writes — both are only provable with contention tests, kept in the default build.
nodes.norm_label: adr 44 — concurrency tests for tenant routing and the async store

nodes.label: ADR 45 — ArchUnit architecture tests
nodes.rationale: Encodes invariants a reviewer would otherwise have to remember: no ThreadLocal inside the async decorator, *Store naming, acyclic slices, and split-package guards.

nodes.label: ADR 46 — PIT mutation testing with a 95% gate
nodes.rationale: Line coverage does not prove the expiry and key boundary logic is actually asserted; a mandated 95% mutation gate (currently 96%, test strength 99%) does, profile-gated so the default build stays fast.
nodes.norm_label: adr 46 — pit mutation testing with a 95% gate

nodes.label: ADR 47 — JDBC insert→update race: bounded retry over silent drop
nodes.rationale: When a concurrent expiry delete removes the row between a failed INSERT and the follow-up UPDATE, the write vanished silently. One bounded re-INSERT (2 attempts max) fixes the common case; losing every attempt is abandoned at warn because the data is a regenerable cache. Native-merge dialects were never affected.
nodes.norm_label: adr 47 — jdbc insert→update race: bounded retry over silent drop

nodes.label: ADR 48 — INFO lifecycle event, DEBUG payload body
nodes.rationale: Serialising the full ReferentialPayload for an INFO log put payload serialisation on the hot path; only the name stays at INFO, the body moves to DEBUG.
nodes.norm_label: adr 48 — info lifecycle event, debug payload body

nodes.label: ADR 49 — Extract scatter/gather collaborators
nodes.rationale: ScatterGatherFailoverHandler became a thin facade over PayloadScatter / PayloadGather / SliceDispatcher / SplitterInvoker; public API and behaviour unchanged, construction moved to a builder instead of overloaded constructors.

nodes.label: ADR 50 — Metrics helper: concatenation over String.format
nodes.rationale: Metric-key construction sat on the recover path; replacing String.format with concatenation plus typed collect overloads made the recover-bag build ~3.6× faster (JMH 744 → 204 ns/op).
nodes.norm_label: adr 50 — metrics helper: concatenation over string.format

nodes.label: ADR 51 — Per-method failover outcome metric
nodes.rationale: failover.recovery.outcome.total{name,domain,method,outcome} gives failover / recovery / non-recovery rates per intercepted method, recorded once per call and tagged by the actual SimpleClass#method.

nodes.label: ADR 52 — Method-aware FailoverHandler contract + AbstractFailoverHandler
nodes.rationale: Threading the intercepted Method through store/recover/recoverAll replaces ADR 51's ad-hoc mechanism; AbstractFailoverHandler bridges method-agnostic handlers so only custom SPI implementations migrate. Accepted as a breaking SPI change because it is the honest contract.

nodes.label: ADR 53 — Cross-module JaCoCo coverage gate
nodes.rationale: Per-module coverage hides gaps at module boundaries; failover-test-report unpacks all classes, merges every exec file and fails verify below 95% line / 95% branch repo-wide.

nodes.label: ADR 54 — Collapse four property-gated store beans into one
nodes.rationale: Four @ConditionalOnProperty variants for the async × multitenant matrix duplicated assembly logic; a single failoverStore bean builds the chain imperatively and makes per-tenant-async explicit. Refines ADR 18, behaviour unchanged.
nodes.norm_label: adr 54 — collapse four property-gated store beans into one

nodes.label: ADR 55 — Embedded Failover Dashboard
nodes.rationale: Operators could only read failover config from source and KPIs from a Prometheus/Grafana stack. A springdoc-style batteries-included panel closes that gap, but an on-by-default operational UI is a security hazard — hence a separate starter, enabled=false by default, no new instrumentation (KPIs derived from existing counters), a vendored CDN-free Chart.js, a fail-closed access gate, and allow-insecure refused outright under the prod profile. History is a process-local ring, deliberately not a TSDB.

nodes.label: ADR 56 — Payload-at-rest encryption for the JDBC store
nodes.rationale: PayloadCipher SPI plus EncryptingSerializer over the JDBC store using an ENC(<cipherId>:…) envelope so ciphertext is self-describing and rotation is a write-switch only; opt-in, and the b64 default is explicitly marked non-secure so nobody mistakes it for encryption.
nodes.norm_label: adr 56 — payload-at-rest encryption for the jdbc store

nodes.label: ADR 57 — Async executor back-pressure
nodes.rationale: Unbounded virtual-thread dispatch has no admission control; BoundedTaskExecutor adds a semaphore guard that keeps tasks on virtual threads (no thread-pool swap), with concurrency-limit plus a rejection-policy (DISCARD default). Unbounded remains the default so existing behaviour is unchanged until configured.

nodes.label: ADR 58 — Non-durable store in production: advisory WARN over fail-fast
nodes.rationale: Profile-aware fail-fast was rejected as brittle (profiles are not a reliable production signal); instead the WARN names jdbc as the recommended production store and points at store decision/topology docs.
nodes.norm_label: adr 58 — non-durable store in production: advisory warn over fail-fast

nodes.label: ADR 59 — Count async submit-time rejection
nodes.rationale: Executor rejection at submit time (ABORT policy or shutdown) was a saturation blind spot; it now emits the existing failover.store.async.failed meter rather than adding a new meter or tag.

nodes.label: ADR 60 — Allowlist strict mode: fail-closed on an empty allowlist
nodes.rationale: ADR 37 left one fail-open edge: an empty resolved allowlist disabled the restriction entirely, so a misconfiguration (scanner found nothing, AOP not wired) silently reopened the gadget surface. strict-allowlist makes empty mean deny-all; introduced false in 2.x and flipped to true in 3.0.0 because a major version is the point to stop shipping the fail-open default. The normal scanner-derived path is unchanged in either mode.
nodes.norm_label: adr 60 — allowlist strict mode: fail-closed on an empty allowlist

nodes.label: ADR 61 — Built-in AES-GCM payload cipher
nodes.rationale: ADR 56 shipped the SPI but only a non-secure b64 default, so real encryption required consumer crypto code. AesGcmPayloadCipher (id aesgcm) auto-registers from failover.store.jdbc.encryption.key to give usable encryption-at-rest out of the box.

nodes.label: ADR 62 — Opt-in JDBC live-entries gauge
nodes.rationale: Capacity visibility needs a row count, but a COUNT(*) per scrape is a real tax on a large table — so FailoverStoreJdbc implements FailoverStoreSizeAware and the gauge is off by default behind live-entries-gauge-enabled.

nodes.label: ADR 63 — Startup warning for un-advisable @Failover placement
nodes.rationale: An @Failover on an interface, a non-public/static/final method or a final class is never advised and fails silently at runtime; the scanner WARNs at startup instead, and self-invocation is documented.
nodes.norm_label: adr 63 — startup warning for un-advisable @failover placement

nodes.label: ADR 64 — Startup warning for recoverAll without a payloadSplitter
nodes.rationale: recoverAll=true with no payloadSplitter silently falls back to single-key recover, so the feature appears configured but does nothing; the scanner WARNs at startup.
nodes.norm_label: adr 64 — startup warning for recoverall without a payloadsplitter

nodes.label: ADR 65 — Event-driven snapshot publishing with throttle and backoff
nodes.rationale: Fixed-interval polling pushed snapshots even when no metric events occurred, and mixed HTTP transport with publish orchestration in the wrong module. Replaced by metric-event-driven pushes throttled to one per interval-seconds via AtomicLong CAS, with WARN-once backoff; SnapshotPushClient abstracts transport so failover-observable-micrometer stays free of spring-web, and BoundedTaskExecutor(limit=1, DISCARD) means a second push while one is in flight is dropped because the in-flight push already carries the latest snapshot.
nodes.norm_label: adr 65 — event-driven snapshot publishing with throttle and backoff

nodes.label: ADR 66 — Decoupled heartbeat liveness tracking
nodes.rationale: Inferring liveness from snapshot freshness conflated 'alive' with 'has recent metric events' (a quiet healthy instance read as DOWN) and used a kilobytes-of-JSON payload as a liveness signal. A separate {"instanceId"} heartbeat drives LiveStatus LIVE/DOWN/UNKNOWN while DOWN instances keep contributing last-known metrics. Polling is correct here — unlike snapshots, heartbeats must fire even with no metric events. Opt-in on both sides, default off.

nodes.label: ADR 67 — Reset-aware aggregate and bounded instance retirement
nodes.rationale: Peer snapshots carry cumulative counters that reset on restart, so the instant aggregate dropped while the trend graph stayed smooth — two views of the same data disagreeing. SnapshotBaseline folds pre-restart totals into a per-instance carry-forward (detected by a drop in cumulative total). Separately, naive eviction would violate the invariant that a dead peer's counts keep contributing, so unseen instances retire into retiredAggregate() and compact into a bounded tombstone past 100 entries — heap stays bounded under pod churn and cluster totals never shrink.
nodes.norm_label: adr 67 — reset-aware aggregate and bounded instance retirement

nodes.label: ADR 68 — Rolling-window dashboard health classification
nodes.rationale: Lifetime-cumulative counters meant an endpoint degraded correctly but never recovered — errors from hours ago kept it DEGRADED after 10,000 clean calls. RollingHealthWindow reconstructs a last-N-calls window by diffing cumulative totals per poll, needing no new instrumentation; deliberately not reusing FailoverApiHealthTracker (different module, hardcoded window, gauge-internals read path). Trade-off: ordering within one poll interval is not preserved. Scoped to the local source; prometheus/shared-store aggregate differently.

nodes.label: ADR 69 — Specific authorization-denial messages for the dashboard gate
nodes.rationale: Spring's default 403 is blank, so an operator who logs in via OIDC but has no GrantedAuthoritiesMapper cannot tell that mapping is the missing piece. DashboardAccessDeniedHandler names the missing role/authority in the body (generic text for EXPRESSION, whose sub-clause failure cannot be introspected) and logs the principal's actual authorities server-side only. Accepted trade-off: the required role string is disclosed, but only to already-authenticated callers.
nodes.norm_label: adr 69 — specific authorization-denial messages for the dashboard gate

nodes.label: ADR 70 — No auto-DDL and a durable heartbeat store for the JDBC tier
nodes.rationale: Four issues at once: (1) a library must not issue CREATE/ALTER against a consumer's database, so auto-DDL is removed outright with no flag, matching failover-store-jdbc which never auto-created FAILOVER_STORE; (2) SharedStore/Jdbc records lacked @ConstructorBinding, so Spring's binder treated the two-constructor record as ambiguous and silently ignored YAML; (3) the process-local HeartbeatStoreInmemory left every peer UNKNOWN when the dashboard is embedded in multiple instances sharing one database, hence HeartbeatStoreJdbc; (4) @ConditionalOnBean across independently-conditioned auto-configurations in different modules is unreliable without an explicit ordering edge — proven with an ApplicationContextRunner in both declaration orders — fixed with @AutoConfiguration(afterName=...). Timestamps moved to TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE with per-dialect precision caps.
nodes.norm_label: adr 70 — no auto-ddl and a durable heartbeat store for the jdbc tier

nodes.label: ADR process: append-only immutable history
nodes.rationale: ADRs are append-only; once accepted content is never changed. Superseded decisions are marked Deprecated with a cross-reference and new decisions always take the next sequential number, so the history stays auditable.

nodes.label: Changelog 3.0.0 (in development)
nodes.rationale: Spring Boot 4.x / Java 21 with virtual threads, fixed-length MD5/UUID keys, split packages eliminated, method-aware FailoverHandler SPI, strict allowlist default flipped to true, dashboard + distributed cluster tiers, payload encryption, and the OSSRH → Central Portal publishing migration. Keep a Changelog format.

nodes.label: Changelog 1.0.0 (initial release)
nodes.rationale: Original surface: @Failover AOP interception, FailoverHandler store/recover/clean, InMemory/Caffeine/JDBC stores, Referential/ReferentialAware, KeyGenerator, ExpiryPolicy, PayloadEnricher, RecoveredPayloadHandler, FailoverReporter, scheduler and Resilience4j integration.

nodes.label: Maven Central publishing migration (OSSRH → Central Portal)
nodes.rationale: s01.oss.sonatype.org is decommissioned and answers HTTP 402, so the EOL nexus-staging-maven-plugin could no longer publish. central-publishing-maven-plugin (publishingServerId=central, autoPublish, waitUntil=published) owns the deploy target via extensions=true; distributionManagement and the release plugin's stagingRepository are removed. Maintainers must mint a new Central Portal user token — retired OSSRH credentials do not authenticate.
nodes.norm_label: maven central publishing migration (ossrh → central portal)

nodes.label: Non-blocking metric publishing (AsyncObservablePublisher)
nodes.rationale: Wraps the composite publisher so every ObservablePublisher (built-in and custom) runs off the caller thread; a bounded queue with drop-on-full (counted as failover.metrics.dropped.total) guarantees metric emission never blocks a @Failover call. Set enabled=false for synchronous, deterministic tests.

nodes.label: Dashboard XSS and peer-ingest hardening
nodes.rationale: Server-supplied strings (referential names, bean ids, exception types, peer-pushed instance ids) were interpolated raw into innerHTML; CSP blocked script execution but inline styles still allow defacement and data-id="${instanceId}" was one quote from attribute breakout. Peer-ingest endpoints now validate instance ids (charset, ≤200 chars, non-blank) and reject summary-less snapshots, and ingest fails fast when snapshot.username is set without a password — {noop} with an empty password authenticated any guessed username while startup logged ingest as secured.

nodes.label: HeartbeatStoreInmemory unbounded-growth fix
nodes.rationale: Every distinct instance id ever POSTed stayed resident for the life of the JVM, leaving one dead entry per rolled pod forever. Now bounded by the same instance-retention window the snapshot store retires on (so nothing reachable from allInstances() is discarded) plus a 10,000-instance ceiling, and it takes a FailoverClock rather than System.currentTimeMillis() so co-located deployments age heartbeats on the same clock as expiry.

nodes.label: Store / Recover Lifecycle
nodes.rationale: Failover sits between a Spring bean and its upstream dependency: on success it saves the result, on failure it serves the last saved result. This keeps recovery transparent so calling code never changes.

nodes.label: Entry Lifecycle States (Live / Stale / Expired)
nodes.rationale: Callers receive upToDate=true in Live and upToDate=false in Stale; expired entries are never served so a caller can never silently act on data past its TTL.

nodes.label: Handler Chain (decorator, built inside-out / invoked outside-in)
nodes.rationale: Three handlers compose as decorators so each concern (metrics, slicing, core store/recover) is independently replaceable via @ConditionalOnMissingBean. The chain is assembled once at startup inside-out and invoked outside-in, making the runtime path the exact reverse of the bean build order. delegateT and delegateR are the same DefaultFailoverHandler instance so composite and per-slice paths share one inner handler and clean() runs once, not twice.
nodes.norm_label: handler chain (decorator, built inside-out / invoked outside-in)

nodes.label: FailoverAspect
nodes.rationale: A Spring AOP @Around advice resolves the reflected Method and hands control to FailoverExecution. Only Exception triggers recovery; java.lang.Error is rethrown unwrapped because recovery itself allocates and must never run on a dying JVM.

nodes.label: FailoverExecution (Basic | Resilience)
nodes.rationale: ResilienceFailoverExecution extends BasicFailoverExecution and only wraps the upstream supplier in a circuit breaker, so the recover path and handler order are identical for both execution types.

nodes.label: AdvancedFailoverHandler
nodes.rationale: Outermost layer: times the call, catches recover-path errors so they never break the caller, publishes metrics, then runs RecoveredPayloadHandler. The is-recovered flag is captured BEFORE RecoveredPayloadHandler so it reflects the true store hit/miss rather than the substituted fallback.

nodes.label: ScatterGatherFailoverHandler
nodes.rationale: Middle layer: splits the composite into per-entity slices when payloadSplitter is set, otherwise a transparent pass-through, so the scatter concern costs nothing when unused.

nodes.label: DefaultFailoverHandler
nodes.rationale: Innermost core: store generates the key, computes expireOn and enriches; recover looks up, checks expiry, enriches and deletes expired entries; clean purges by expiry.

nodes.label: ReferentialPayload envelope
nodes.rationale: A single envelope (name, key, upToDate, asOf, expireOn, payload) wraps every stored entry so metadata travels with the data through every store backend.

nodes.label: Defensive copy contract on FailoverStore.find()
nodes.rationale: find() must return a copy, not a live reference, because callers mutate upToDate and asOf on the returned object; without a copy those mutations would corrupt the persisted entry. See ADR 10.

nodes.label: ReferentialAware (interface)
nodes.rationale: Interface alternative to the Referential base class for domain types that already have a superclass and cannot inherit.

nodes.label: Store Assembly Chain (Async -> MultiTenant -> base)
nodes.rationale: DefaultFailoverStore (defensive copy) always wraps the raw store; FailoverStoreAsync is added when failover.store.async=true. In multi-tenant mode MultiTenantFailoverStore is outermost and async sits inside it per tenant, because the tenant must be resolved on the calling thread before any executor boundary. See ADR 18 and ADR 54.

nodes.label: FailoverAutoConfiguration failoverHandler assembly
nodes.rationale: Every bean is @ConditionalOnMissingBean so any layer of the chain can be replaced by a user bean without forking the framework.

nodes.label: Method identity threading (@NonNull Method, ADR 52)
nodes.rationale: The reflected Method is threaded @NonNull through the whole chain down to each scatter slice even though only AdvancedFailoverHandler consumes it (to tag per-method metrics). Threading it uniformly avoids null checks and lets any future decorator tag by method.

nodes.label: Three-Layer Key Architecture
nodes.rationale: Only Layer 1 (KeyGenerator) is user-controlled; Layers 2 (UUID hashing) and 3 (store keying) are automatic, so application code never has to think about column widths or namespacing.

nodes.label: DefaultKeyGenerator
nodes.rationale: Args are converted to a raw string joined by ':'. Types with an identity toString() fall back to ClassName@hexHashCode, which is unstable across restarts, so a WARN is logged once per type (once, to avoid flooding the hot path).

nodes.label: FailoverKeyGenerator (UUID hashing, Layer 2)
nodes.rationale: UUID.nameUUIDFromBytes(effectiveName + ':' + rawKey) yields a fixed 36-char key: it prevents VARCHAR(256) overflow in the JDBC store, obscures business data at rest, and is deterministic so the same inputs always resolve the same entry.

nodes.label: FailoverNameResolver / effectiveName
nodes.rationale: effectiveName = domain.isBlank() ? name : domain. Two annotations sharing a domain hash with the same namespace prefix and store under the same FAILOVER_NAME, enabling cross-failover sharing. Logging still uses name (not effectiveName) so log lines stay distinguishable within a domain.

nodes.label: Key Stability Requirement
nodes.rationale: The same args must produce the same key at store and recover time, on every instance and across restarts. Pitfalls: identity toString/hashCode, unordered collections (Set iteration order), non-deterministic components (timestamps, request ids), and collisions from incomplete business identifiers.

nodes.label: Custom KeyGenerator bean
nodes.rationale: A custom generator completely replaces DefaultKeyGenerator — there is no partial delegation — so normalisation (sorting CSV, uppercasing) must be done wholly inside it.

nodes.label: ENC(<id>:<ciphertext>) self-describing envelope
nodes.rationale: ENC( is a reserved marker no plaintext JSON value can start with. Recording the cipher id in the row gives three properties: self-describing reads (decryptor chosen from the row, not config), mixed plaintext/b64/aesgcm stores that all read back correctly (foundation for rotation), and safe toggling since enabling/disabling changes only new writes.

nodes.label: EncryptingSerializer
nodes.rationale: Encryption is a decorator over the Serializer — the single boundary where a payload becomes a persisted string — so it transforms only the PAYLOAD column and leaves the rest of the failover flow untouched. Scoped to JDBC because only that store persists a string.

nodes.label: PayloadCipher SPI
nodes.rationale: Ciphers deal in raw ciphertext only; the EncryptingSerializer owns the envelope so implementors never parse it. id() must be unique and contain neither ':' nor ')' because it is persisted in every row — changing it strands existing rows.

nodes.label: Cipher registry (read) + active write cipher
nodes.rationale: All PayloadCipher beans are indexed by id() for reads while exactly one, chosen by failover.store.jdbc.encryption.cipher, is the active write cipher. An unknown id on read raises FailoverStoreException rather than returning garbage.

nodes.label: Base64PayloadCipher (id b64)
nodes.rationale: Zero-dependency default and worked example of the SPI, providing no confidentiality — a loud WARN fires when it is the active write cipher. It is given a cipher id specifically so mismatches fail loudly: a bare Base64 decoder would happily 'decode' AES ciphertext into garbage and surface a confusing JSON error three layers away.

nodes.label: Encryption vs. deserialization allowlist orthogonality
nodes.rationale: PAYLOAD (data) is encrypted but PAYLOAD_CLASS (type name) is not, so on read the payload is decrypted first and the allowlist still gates class loading on the real plaintext class name. Encryption hides data; the allowlist constrains which classes may be instantiated.

nodes.label: What payload encryption is not
nodes.rationale: Not transport security, not a substitute for DB/disk encryption or access control (defense in depth only), not key management (your PayloadCipher owns the keys), and not available for non-JDBC stores.

nodes.label: Scatter / Gather
nodes.rationale: Single-key storage of a collection means one upstream failure wipes every cached entry at once and partial recovery is impossible. Scatter/gather stores each entity under its own key. It is the most involved feature, so the guidance is to default to single-key @Failover unless per-entity slicing (independent expiry/recovery, partial recovery) is genuinely needed.

nodes.label: Parallel slice dispatch (virtual threads)
nodes.rationale: Per-entity store/recover run as a CompletableFuture per slice on virtual threads by default; sequential mode exists for debugging and low-throughput scenarios.

nodes.label: Per-slice timeout (failover.scatter.timeout)
nodes.rationale: Without a bound, one hung slice (e.g. exhausted JDBC pool) blocks the business thread indefinitely on join(). On recover the timeout is per slice and a timed-out slice counts as not recovered so the rest still merges; on store it bounds aggregate completion (allOf().orTimeout()) and already-completed writes are not rolled back. Ignored when parallel=false because inline slices cannot be interrupted.

nodes.label: Partial Recovery Behaviour
nodes.rationale: The framework never filters nulls — merge owns the null policy — and only short-circuits to null when every slice is empty. Partial recovery is logged as a WARN and metered via failover.recovery.partial.total so it is never silent. In some domains an incomplete collection is more dangerous than a clean failure because the caller cannot tell it is incomplete, so rejecting the whole composite is a documented option.

nodes.label: recoverAll semantics (four rules)
nodes.rationale: shouldRecoverAll = args == null || args.isEmpty() || recoverAll(). recoverAll affects only the recover path (store always splits); empty args recover-all automatically; id args need no flag; filter args must force recoverAll=true or the filters would be wrongly split into entity keys. recoverAll without a payloadSplitter does nothing and logs a startup WARN.

nodes.label: N-slice recover-all deduplication rule
nodes.rationale: doRecoverAll calls recoverSliceForAll per context; with the default handler recoverAll ignores args and returns all entries by name, so N contexts produce N x all-entries. splitOnRecover must therefore return exactly one placeholder unless a custom delegateR.recoverAll partitions by the context args.

nodes.label: Two-splitter pattern (batch-by-id + findAll on one domain)
nodes.rationale: A method with id args and a separate findAll() need different recover strategies, so they use two PayloadSplitter beans but share a domain — each populates entries the other can recover.
nodes.norm_label: two-splitter pattern (batch-by-id + findall on one domain)

nodes.label: PayloadSplitterExecutionException
nodes.rationale: Wraps any user-splitter failure with operation, splitter bean name, failover name, full annotation config and original cause, so a splitter bug is diagnosable from logs without a debugger.

nodes.label: Failover Properties Reference
nodes.rationale: There are no mandatory properties — the framework starts with production-safe defaults.

nodes.label: failover.store.async + async-executor back-pressure
nodes.rationale: Writes (store/delete/cleanByExpiry) are offloaded to a virtual-thread executor while find is always synchronous because the caller needs the recovered value immediately. concurrency-limit + rejection-policy (DISCARD/CALLER_RUNS/ABORT) bound the blast radius; DISCARD is the default because the store is a regenerable cache.

nodes.label: failover.store.jdbc.strict-allowlist
nodes.rationale: Changed to true in 3.0.0: an empty resolved allowlist now denies all deserialization (fail-closed) instead of disabling the restriction. Affects only the degenerate case where nothing was discovered and nothing configured.

nodes.label: Observable properties (async publish, instance tag, cardinality guard)
nodes.rationale: Metrics publish off the caller thread via a bounded queue so emitting a metric can never block a @Failover call; a full queue drops the metric (counted) rather than back-pressuring. instance.mode=auto tags every registry except Prometheus (which adds instance at scrape). The cardinality guard caps distinct name values so a misconfigured name cannot explode the registry.
nodes.norm_label: observable properties (async publish, instance tag, cardinality guard)

nodes.label: Dashboard properties (secure-by-default)
nodes.rationale: enabled defaults to false and is the only switch needed; exposure flags only narrow. allow-insecure is refused outright under the prod profile so production can never silently disable the access gate.

nodes.label: Dashboard cluster properties (local | prometheus | shared-store)
nodes.rationale: Peer-side snapshot.jdbc.enabled (direct write) is mutually exclusive with publish-url (HTTP push) and setting both fails fast at startup. Liveness needs both the dashboard-side and peer-side toggles because the dashboard cannot read a peer's config.

nodes.label: Choosing a Store
nodes.rationale: Failover only protects callers if the last-known-good value still exists when upstream fails. A non-durable store holds it in one JVM's heap, lost on restart and invisible to other instances — so the choice is driven by deployment topology and tolerance for losing cached data.

nodes.label: InMemory store
nodes.rationale: Size-capped by default (max-entries 10000, LRU eviction) so high-cardinality keys cannot grow the heap without bound. Dev/test only — a restart loses everything.

nodes.label: Caffeine store
nodes.rationale: Handles its own eviction from ReferentialPayload.expireOn so entries expire without the cleanup scheduler. Capped at max-size 10000 (Window TinyLFU). The module deliberately does not bundle Caffeine — the version is managed by spring-boot-dependencies.

nodes.label: JDBC store
nodes.rationale: The only built-in durable, shared store and the recommended production choice; it is what makes failover 'clustered' since there is no special cluster mode, just shared durable state. Dialect detection is automatic via DatabaseResolver. No JDBC driver is bundled so consumers pick their own.

nodes.label: EXPIRE_ON index requirement
nodes.rationale: The hourly cleanup DELETE ... WHERE EXPIRE_ON < ? degrades to a full table scan without an index on EXPIRE_ON, so the index is mandated in the DDL (audit I-13).

nodes.label: JDBC capacity planning
nodes.rationale: One upsert per successful protected call means write volume scales with success throughput x instances. Bound it with async-executor concurrency-limit, keep TTL short, run expiry cleanup, and optionally enable the failover.live.entries gauge (off by default because it costs a COUNT(*) per scrape).

nodes.label: Deployment topologies and orthogonal modes
nodes.rationale: Store choice, clustering, multi-tenancy and async writes are orthogonal and compose — a clustered, multi-tenant, async JDBC store is the typical production setup. Store clustering (use JDBC) is a separate concern from dashboard cluster aggregation modes.

nodes.label: name vs. domain
nodes.rationale: name identifies this failover point (metric label, default store grouping) and must be unique per method; domain deliberately groups methods so they share store entries. Rule of thumb: set only name until two methods genuinely need to read each other's stored data.

nodes.label: Production shape: JDBC store + JDBC shared-store direct write
nodes.source_location: ## 7. Add the Dashboard (JDBC Store + JDBC Shared-Store, Direct Write)
nodes.rationale: Putting the @Failover store, the dashboard cluster aggregate and peer snapshot writes in one database removes the ingest endpoint and its auth entirely; every replica runs the identical YAML pointed at the same DB. Neither dashboard table is created by the module — DDL is the consumer's responsibility.
nodes.norm_label: production shape: jdbc store + jdbc shared-store direct write

nodes.label: @Failover placement rules (CGLIB proxy)
nodes.rationale: The annotation only works where the AOP proxy can intercept: public, non-static, non-final method on a non-final concrete bean, called from another bean. Interface beans (Feign, Spring Data, @HttpExchange) are the exception since Spring uses a JDK interface proxy there. A startup WARN flags un-advisable concrete-class placements; self-invocation is a runtime call-graph property and cannot be detected statically.

nodes.label: Expression-based expiry (expiryDurationExpression / expiryUnitExpression)
nodes.rationale: Expressions resolve from properties, environment variables or any Spring EL, and take priority over the fixed attributes, so expiry can differ per profile/environment without recompiling.

nodes.label: Domain grouping on @Failover
nodes.rationale: All annotations in one domain must agree on expiry — a mismatch makes the last writer overwrite the stored expiry timestamp, so a startup WARN is logged when detected.

nodes.label: @Failover attribute resolution order
nodes.rationale: Non-blank expression attributes override their fixed counterparts; expiryPolicy overrides the default policy but expiryDuration/expiryUnit still supply defaults when the policy delegates; keyGenerator overrides the default generator; payloadSplitter enables scatter/gather mode.

nodes.label: RETHROW exception policy
nodes.rationale: Default because callers usually must know the upstream is unavailable and cannot gracefully handle a null response.

nodes.label: NEVER_THROW exception policy
nodes.rationale: Suppressing the upstream exception masks outages — the caller cannot tell from the return value — so metrics (recovery.outcome not_recovered, user.impact blocked) become the monitoring signal and a startup WARN fires when it is active.

nodes.label: Error is never recovered
nodes.rationale: Deliberate fail-fast: java.lang.Error signals a JVM-fatal condition, not 'upstream is down', so the process should be recycled by the platform rather than limp on serving stale data — and the recovery path itself allocates, which must not run on a dying JVM.

nodes.label: failover.recovery.outcome.total (per-method outcome counter)
nodes.rationale: One counter recorded once per intercepted method call (a findAll() is one event, not one per entity) yields all three operational rates. It is tagged by method so two methods sharing a name/domain stay distinguishable, and 'error' is kept distinct from 'not_recovered' so a store/serialization fault is never miscounted as a clean miss.

nodes.label: FailoverMeterBinder gauges
nodes.rationale: failover.live.entries is registered only when the store can report size — always for in-memory/Caffeine, JDBC only when opted in, because it costs a SELECT COUNT(*) per scrape (audit A7). Not available in multi-tenant mode.

nodes.label: failover.store.async.failed counter
nodes.rationale: Async write failures are swallowed so they never break the business call, which would silently degrade the store layer — this counter keeps that visible. It covers both in-flight failure and submit-time rejection, closing the gap where a saturated executor dropped writes unmetered. DISCARD deliberately does not increment it because discarding is configured behaviour, not a failure; use ABORT if every dropped write must be alertable.

nodes.label: Kibana dashboard via micrometer-registry-elastic
nodes.rationale: The elastic registry pushes existing failover.* meters, so Kibana visualizations need no additional instrumentation.

nodes.label: Structured log levels (INFO name-only, DEBUG full payload)
nodes.rationale: Lifecycle events stay at INFO carrying only the referential name and the full payload body moved to DEBUG so high-throughput services pay no full-payload serialisation on the INFO path (ADR 48).
nodes.norm_label: structured log levels (info name-only, debug full payload)

nodes.label: AesGcmPayloadCipher (id aesgcm)
nodes.source_location: ## Real encryption out of the box: AES-GCM (recommended)
nodes.rationale: AES-GCM authenticated encryption with a random IV per write and a 128-bit tag, auto-registered when failover.store.jdbc.encryption.key is non-empty; an invalid key fails startup fast. Being authenticated it throws on a tampered row or wrong key rather than returning corrupted data.

nodes.label: Cipher / key rotation procedure
nodes.rationale: Because each row records its cipher id, rotation is rolling: add the new cipher alongside the old, point writes at it, let old rows decrypt via the retained bean, drop the old bean once they expire. A row naming an unregistered cipher throws FailoverStoreException, which is acceptable because the store is a disposable cache.

nodes.label: Encryption operational notes (column sizing, lookups, key secrecy)
nodes.rationale: Ciphertext is larger than plaintext so PAYLOAD must be sized up. Lookups are unaffected because the store key is FAILOVER_NAME + FAILOVER_KEY, not the payload, so a random-IV ciphertext does not break find. The key must come from a secret manager; losing it only costs a cold start since the store is regenerable.
nodes.norm_label: encryption operational notes (column sizing, lookups, key secrecy)

nodes.label: AbstractListPayloadSplitter<T>
nodes.rationale: Collapses a full splitter to the one thing that differs per use case — the slice key — by fixing T=List<T>, R=T and supplying working defaults for splitIntoSlices, keyArgsToRecover and mergeSlices.

nodes.label: AbstractPayloadSplitter<T, R>
nodes.rationale: For a wrapper composite rather than a bare List: you implement splitIntoSlices to unwrap and mergeSlices to re-wrap, but still skip the context plumbing.

nodes.label: Slice-key contract (keyArgsForSlice vs keyArgsToRecover)
nodes.rationale: Store-side and recover-side args must derive the same store key for the same entity; if they diverge a slice is stored under one key and looked up under another and recovery silently returns nothing. This is why CSV tokens must be parsed to the stored key type (Long, not String), and why filters are excluded from the key so the entity can be shared across methods in a domain.

nodes.label: Defensive arg reading in keyArgsToRecover / splitOnRecover
nodes.rationale: Blind args.get(0) or casts throw on empty/null/wrong-typed args and then the splitter fails for every recovery; guard with the instanceof pattern and return an empty list, which the framework treats as 'no slices' (warn + skip) rather than an error.
nodes.norm_label: defensive arg reading in keyargstorecover / splitonrecover

nodes.label: Merge null policy (positional / compact / reject)
nodes.source_location: ## Partial Recovery: Null Policy in merge
nodes.rationale: Slices arrive in the same order splitOnRecover emitted them, so position carries meaning. Option A keeps nulls positionally when the caller maps results back by index, Option B compacts when the caller just wants what is available, Option C returns null on any miss when a partial list is unsafe. A cache miss, an expired entry and a timed-out slice are indistinguishable at merge — all null.

nodes.label: Splitter failures stay inside the failover boundary
nodes.source_location: ## Splitter failures stay inside the failover boundary
nodes.rationale: On the store path the exception is logged at ERROR and the real business result is returned unchanged, so a splitter bug never breaks a working upstream call; on the recover path recovery yields null and flows to RecoveredPayloadHandler and the ExceptionPolicy as a normal non-recovery. Users write no try/catch.

nodes.label: FailoverHandler<T> interface
nodes.rationale: Every operation carries the intercepted @NonNull Method so the outermost handler can tag metrics per method.

nodes.label: AbstractFailoverHandler
nodes.rationale: Bridges the method-aware contract to method-less protected operations so handlers that do not need the Method stay simple; decorators that tag per-method metrics implement FailoverHandler directly (ADR 52).

nodes.label: RecoveredPayloadHandler interface
nodes.rationale: Last-chance hook called by AdvancedFailoverHandler when the inner handler returns null and exception-policy is never_throw, so a safe default can replace null.

nodes.label: ContextPropagator interface
nodes.rationale: Propagates thread-local context (tenant, MDC) across virtual-thread executor boundaries in scatter/gather; multiple beans are composed into a CompositeContextPropagator.
